title: Hardware and disk space management
lead: DBMS layers, storage hierarchy, page I/O and the disk space manager.

sections.title: DBMS architecture
sections.html:
Layer interfaces and cross-cutting services

LayerResponsibility
PlanningSQL → checked physical plan
ExecutionPlan → record streams
Files/indexesRecords/RIDs → logical pages
Buffer managerPage ID → pinned memory frame
Disk space managerPage ID → file/device location

Each interface permits its caller to reason at a higher level. The execution engine need not know disk offsets, and the disk manager need not understand SQL attributes. Concurrency control and recovery cross these boundaries because locking, memory updates, log persistence and data-page persistence must be coordinated. The repeated architecture figures introduce one layer at a time; they are stages of one stack, not separate systems.

PDF pp. 1–10

sections.title: Storage hierarchy and magnetic disks
sections.html:
Volatility, granularity and latency hierarchy

Disk-oriented systems process values in RAM but persist pages on storage. Byte-addressable RAM permits direct field access; block interfaces transfer a whole page. Capacity, cost per byte, latency and volatility all affect placement.

The slide’s illustrative latencies are registers below 1 ns, cache below 10 ns, DRAM around 100 ns, SSD around 0.1 ms, HDD around 10 ms and network storage around 30 ms. These orders of magnitude explain caching; the quoted storage prices and capacities are historical examples. An in-memory database still requires a durability mechanism and is not automatically safe from power loss.

PDF pp. 11–14

HDD access calculation

A disk has rotating platters, tracks, sectors and heads moved by an arm. Access time = seek + rotational wait + transfer. At 15,000 rpm, one rotation is 60/15000 seconds = 4 ms, so a random arrival waits half a rotation on average: 2 ms.

For the source drive, an 8 KB transfer at approximately 163 MB/s takes about 0.05 ms. Adding 3.4 ms seek gives 5.45 ms per random block. The 512 KB/track detail limits how far a sequential run remains on one track. Transfer time alone is not the cost of a random HDD read.

PDF pp. 15–17

A thousand random versus sequential blocks

For 1000 source blocks, random access costs about 1000·5.45 ms = 5.45 s. Sequential access pays positioning once and then mostly transfer: 3.4 + 2 + 1000·0.05 ≈ 55.4 ms, plus small track-transition overheads.

Arrange neighbouring logical pages on nearby disk locations and prefetch consecutive pages to amortise positioning. This is a placement strategy and a workload-dependent benefit, not a guarantee that every logical successor is physically adjacent on an arbitrary filesystem.

PDF pp. 18–19

sections.title: SSDs and page-oriented storage
sections.html:
Flash erase blocks and write amplification

NAND reads and programs pages but erases larger blocks. Updating a small logical region can require copying live content and erasing/reclaiming a larger physical region. Physical bytes written can therefore exceed application bytes written: write amplification.

Finite erase endurance motivates wear levelling. SSDs remove HDD head movements, yet random writes can remain less efficient than sequential writes because of mapping, buffering and garbage collection. The source’s bandwidth/price figures describe its example devices, not constants for every SSD. Both device type and locality belong in a refined cost model.

PDF pp. 20–23

Files, pages, records and control objectives

A file comprises pages; a page contains records. This course uses page and block for the transfer granularity and counts a page read or write as one I/O in simplified models.

Spatial control chooses where to place pages used together. Temporal control chooses when to read or flush pages to minimise stalls and preserve correctness. A system can manage a database larger than RAM by moving only required pages, reusing cached pages and scheduling transfers. Larger pages amortise transfer overhead but can carry more unused data.

PDF pp. 24–25

sections.title: Disk space manager
sections.html:
Page allocation and physical mappings

The disk space manager exposes allocatePage, freePage, readPage and writePage. A page ID is a logical identifier, typically mapping to a filename and byte offset; it is not the record’s SQL key. The source cites page sizes around 4–64 KB.

A logical file can span several OS files or devices. Allocating a large filesystem file is one implementation; older DBMSs also used raw storage. A sequential request expresses expected locality, which the allocation policy tries to provide. Upper layers depend on that abstraction while remaining unaware of filesystem sectors or device addresses.

PDF pp. 26–29

quiz.question: Under the exercise’s model, how long does reading 200 contiguous pages take?
quiz.explanation: Seek time plus rotational latency is 7 ms. Transferring 200 pages takes 20 ms, giving a total of 27 ms under the stated assumptions.
